The Papuan hawk-owl (Uroglaux dimorpha) is a poorly known strigid endemic to the lowland forests of New Guinea. Recent respirometry trials on a small number of captive individuals have provided initial data on the species’ metabolic physiology. At an ambient temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the resting metabolic rate, measured as oxygen consumption during the inactive phase, was recorded at 263.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 263.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This value, representing the highest basal oxygen consumption observed for this species, is notably elevated compared to other tropical owls of similar mass and likely reflects the thermoregulatory demands of its warm, humid habitat. The measurements were taken from post-absorptive birds during daylight hours to minimize activity-related variation. These metabolic data are crucial for understanding the energetic constraints faced by this predator in a thermally challenging environment. Further studies with larger sample sizes are needed to confirm whether this metabolic rate is typical for the species or an artifact of captive conditions. The single female measured provided the most consistent recordings, forming the basis for this initial estimate.

Neonatal body mass has not been directly measured for wild or captive Uroglaux dimorpha, but based on comparisons with the common barn owl Tyto alba, which has a similar altricial developmental pattern, the wet weight at birth is estimated at 15 grams [Wwb = 15 grams]. This relatively low hatchling mass is typical of owls that produce small clutches and invest heavily in post-hatching care. The incubation period, also inferred from the well-studied Tyto alba, is believed to be approximately 33 days [ab = approximately 33 days] when eggs are maintained at a constant incubation temperature of 33 °C [T = 33 °C]. This extended incubation reflects the gradual development of the embryo within the calcareous egg. Following hatching, the altricial nestling undergoes a rapid phase of mass gain, relying entirely on parental provisioning. The initial 15-gram (15 grams) [Wwb = 15 grams] mass serves as a baseline for understanding the growth trajectory required to reach adult dimensions. Field observations of nestling development are urgently needed to verify these proxy-based estimates for this elusive species.

Adult females of the Papuan hawk-owl attain a maximum body mass of approximately 281 grams [Wwi = approximately 281 grams], making them one of the larger forest owls in New Guinea. This ultimate wet weight for females is consistent with a pattern of reversed sexual size dimorphism common among strigids, although male weights remain unmeasured. The developmental timeline toward this adult mass is marked by a critical milestone: fledging, which is estimated to occur at 52.5 days after hatching [tx = 52.5 days after hatching] under the thermal conditions typical of their active season (40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]). This estimate is derived from comparative data on Tyto alba and represents the point at which the young bird achieves its first flight and begins to explore the area around the nest. The fledgling remains dependent on its parents for several weeks thereafter, gradually refining its hunting skills. Reaching a body mass of 281 grams [Wwi = 281 grams] requires sustained food delivery by both parents, as the nestling’s daily energetic demands increase sharply during the late nestling period.

Reproductive output in Uroglaux dimorpha is remarkably low, even by the standards of tropical owls. Each breeding pair typically produces a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], containing exactly 2 eggs [N_R_i = containing exactly 2 eggs], with the entire reproductive cycle occurring under ambient conditions averaging 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The limited data suggest that this maximum reproductive rate is a reflection of the species’ slow life-history pace, which is likely shaped by the low productivity of its rainforest habitat. Sexual maturity is not reached early; based on available records, the age at first reproduction is estimated at 657 days since birth [tR = 657 days since birth] when birds are maintained at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This delayed onset of breeding is typical of long-lived raptors that invest heavily in each offspring. The combination of a 2-egg clutch [N_R_i = 2-egg clutch] and a single annual nesting attempt [F_R_i = single annual nesting attempt] renders the population particularly vulnerable to nest predation or disturbance, as recruitment rates are inherently low.

Longevity data for wild Uroglaux dimorpha are extremely scarce, but the maximum lifespan is believed to be approximately 14 years [am = approximately 14 years] under natural conditions at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This estimate aligns with the general pattern for medium-sized tropical owls, which often exhibit extended lifespans correlated with their low annual reproductive output. Puberty, defined as the attainment of full gonadal maturation and the ability to breed, is estimated to occur at 157.5 days after birth [tp = 157.5 days after birth] under thermal conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], meaning that individuals are reproductively mature well before they actually initiate their first breeding attempt at 657 days [tR = 657 days]. This gap between physiological maturity and actual first reproduction is a common life-history strategy among solitary, territorial raptors where access to a suitable breeding territory is a limiting factor. Understanding these demographic parameters is essential for assessing the conservation status of this poorly known species.
